text_blocks.snippet: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is typically managed through a combination of heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications.
snippet_highlighted_words: heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when necessary, prescription medications

text_blocks.snippet: Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with high blood pressure and can sometimes reduce the need for or dosage of medications:

list.snippet: Dietary Approaches: Adopt the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fats.
Sodium Reduction: Lower daily salt and sodium intake (ideally aiming for under 1,500 to 2,000 mg per day).
Regular Exercise: Engage in regular aerobic activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, for at least 30 minutes most days.
Weight Management: Lose extra weight if you are overweight or obese to decrease the strain on your heart and blood vessels.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce alcohol consumption and stop smoking or using tobacco products, which constrict blood vessels and raise heart rates.
Stress Management: Practice relaxation or stress-reduction techniques and aim for 7 to 8 hours of quality sleep per night.

text_blocks.snippet: If lifestyle changes alone do not lower your blood pressure to your target goal (generally less than 130/80 mm Hg for most adults), your doctor may prescribe one or more medications.
The primary first-line classes of blood pressure medications include:

list.snippet: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors: Keep blood vessels from narrowing by blocking the formation of a natural chemical that tightens them (e.g., lisinopril, benazepril).
Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax blood vessels by blocking the action—rather than the formation—of that same narrowing chemical (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering the muscle cells of your heart and blood vessels, allowing the vessels to relax and widen (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Thiazide Diuretics: Often called "water pills," these help your kidneys remove excess sodium and water from your body, lowering blood volume (e.g., chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide).
Beta-Blockers: Lower the heart rate and the heart's output of blood; often prescribed if you also have coronary artery disease or heart failure.
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists & Vasodilators: Sometimes added if blood pressure remains high despite multi-drug treatment (resistant hypertension).

text_blocks.snippet: Note: Many people require a combination of two or more blood pressure drugs—sometimes available in a single, fixed-dose pill—to reach their target safely.

You can explore official educational tools and treatment navigators through the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), review medication categories with the American Heart Association, or track guidelines via the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
